title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Dot plot: geom_dotplot()
Width of dot corresponds to the bin width (or max width, depending on binning algorithm), and dots are stacked, with each dot representing one observation.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(dotsize = 0.5)














WarningBe careful



The y scale is not very useful and in fact is misleading. As such it is better to turn off y-axis using scale_y_continous().



ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=2, dotsize = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)














Note



The difference in the first and the second code is the additional binwidth argument. The binwidth controls the binning. The dotsize is scaling the drawing of the dots. So just having binwidth argument means binning is controlled and ggplot automatically default the dot size to 1, as shown below. Having only the dotsize argument means ggplot bins according to its default but size of the dot is controlled as shown in the first code. And having both arguments means that ggplot have to follow the binning and size of the dot specified as shown in the second code.



ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = 2.5)

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Histograms: geom_histograms()
The code chunk below is an example to create a simple histogram by using values in MATHS field of exam_data

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram()

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Density: geom_density()
geom_density() computes and plots kernel density estimate, which is smoothed version of the histogram. Useful alternative to the histogram for continuous data that comes from an underlying smooth distribution.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_density()

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Boxplot: geom_boxplot()
geom_boxplot() displays continous value list. It visualises five summary statistics (the median, two hinges and two whiskers), and all “outlying” points individually.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot()








Notches are used in box plots to help visually assess whether medians of distributions differ. If the notches do not overlap, this is evidence that the medians are different.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE)








From this, it can be seen that the median is not the same.

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Violin plot: geom_violin()
geom_violin() creates violin plot which is a way to compare multiple data distributions. With ordinary density curves, it is difficult to compare more than just a few distributions because the lines visually interfere with each other. With a violin plot, it’s easier to compare several distributions since they’re placed side by side.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER)) +
  geom_violin()

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point()

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
section: Modifying geometric object by changing geom()
text:
Modifying geometric object by changing geom()
Lets use histogram as an example. Bins argument is the number of bins. Fill argument is the shade of the histogram. Color is the outline color of the bars. So, the code below means that the number of bins is 20, with light blue shade outlined with black.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, color='black', fill='light blue')

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
section: Modifying geometric object by changing aes()
text:
Modifying geometric object by changing aes()
We could add a subgroup by using colour, fill, shape argument in aes().

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           colour = GENDER)) +
  geom_density()









ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, color='black')









ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           y = ENGLISH, 
           shape = GENDER)) +
  geom_point()














Note



Scatterplot can use shape and colour. Bar and histogram can use fill. Density can use colour. Dot plot can use shape, colour and fill. Alpha can also be used in aes() which controls the opacity.

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
geom objects can be combined
The code chunk below combine scatterplot and boxplot.

ggplot (data=exam_data,
        aes(y = MATHS, 
            x = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(position='jitter', size = 0.5)














Note



Jitter is used for the position so that a random noise is given to very point, which can prevent overplotting where dots might overlap.

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
stat_summary() method
Below is a simple boxplot that is incomplete because the positions of the means are not shown.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER))+
  geom_boxplot()








Now add stat_summary() function and override default geom.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER))+
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(geom = 'point',
               fun = 'mean',
               colour = 'red',
               size = 4)

text:
geom() method

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER))+
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat = 'summary',
             fun = 'mean',
             colour = 'red',
             size = 4)

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
section: Adding best fit curve on scatterplot
text:
Adding best fit curve on scatterplot
Below is a scatterplot between Maths and English grades of students.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point()








The interpretability of this graph can be improved by adding a best fit curve. This is done using geom_smooth().

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(size = 0.5)








The default smoothing method used is loess. But this can be overridden as shown below.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5)

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
facet_wrap() function
facet_wrap() wraps a 1d sequence of panels into 2d. This is generally a better use of screen spae than facet_grid() because most displays are roughly rectangular.
The code chunk below plots a trellis plot using facet_wrap().

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_wrap(~ CLASS)








It is also possible to do a combination as shown in the code chunk below.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_wrap(~ CLASS + GENDER)

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
facet_grid() function
facet_grid() forms a matrix of panels defined by row and column facetting variables. It is most useful when you have two discrete variables, and all combinations of the variables exits in the data.
The code chink below plots a trellis plot using facet_grid().

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_grid(~ GENDER)








The graph plot the trellis plot through column. It is possible to change the orientation to rows instead.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(GENDER))








Again it is possible to do a combination as shown in the code chunk below.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_grid(vars(CLASS), vars(GENDER))

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
coord_flip() function
By default, bar chart of ggplot2 is in vertical form.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar()








The code chunk below flips the horizontal bar chart into vertical bar chart by using coord_flip().

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip()

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
coord_cartesian() function
The scatterplot below is slightly misleading because the y-axis and the x-axis range are not equal.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5)








Lets fix both the y-axis and x-axis range from 0-100. The code chunk below does that.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100),
                  ylim = c(0,100))

title: Hands-on Exercise 2 - Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
ggtheme package
ggtheme provides ggplot2 themes that replicate the look fo plots by Edward Tufte, Stephen Few, Fivethirteight, The Economist, Stata, Excel and The Wall Street Journal among others.
The code below used The Exonomist theme.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths score") +
  theme_economist()














Tip



It has many themes and provides some extra geoms and scales for ggplot2. Consult this site to see the various options.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2 - Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
hrbrthemes packages
hrbrthemes package provides base theme that focuses on typograohic elements including where various lables are placed as well as the fonts that are used.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths score") +
  theme_ipsum()








The second goal centers around productivity for a production workflow where presenting something needs to be visually clean and readable to increase reader’s engagement. Consult this site to learn more.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths score") +
  theme_ipsum(axis_title_size = 18,
              base_size = 15,
              grid = 'Y')














TipWhat can be learnt from the code chunk above?




axis_title_size: controls font size of the axis title
base_size: controls the size of axis label
grid: controls the lines in the graph, in this case remove the x-axis grid lines

text:
patchwork methods
There are several extension function that support composite figure by combining several graphs such as grid.arrange() of gridExtra package and plot_grid() of cowplot package. This section will focus on an extension called patchwork which is specially designed for combining ggplot2 graphs into a single figure.
Patchwok package has a very simple syntax wherewe can create layouts super easily. Here’s the general syntax:

Two-column layout using the plus sign +
Subplot group ysing paranthesis ()
Two-row layout using division sign /
Plot beside each other using |

Examples:

Combine 2 ggplot graphscombine 3 ggplot graphs



p1 + p2











(p1 / p2) | p3

















Tip



Another way is to use wrap_plots() to directly plot all the graphs into one section. Use #| fig-width and #| fig-height to change the size or scale of the figure. This one uses 15 and 7 respectively.

wrap_plots(p1, p2, p3)










To learn more, refer to Plot Assembly. The site has information about adding a table or some text and how to place it to the left of the graph.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2 - Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
Creating composite figure with tag
In order to identify subplots in text, patchwork also provides auto-tagging capabilities as shown below.

((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'I')

title: Hands-on Exercise 2 - Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
Creating figure with inser
It is also possible to insert one or more plots or graphic elements freely on top or below another plot using inset_element().

p3 + inset_element(p2, 
                   left = 0.02, 
                   bottom = 0.7, 
                   right = 0.5, 
                   top = 1,
                   align_to = 'full')














Note



align_to specifies where the element should be relative to. ‘panel’ is the default, ‘full’ is for the whole image, ‘plot’ is for the plot area of the main layer.

section: Creating composite figure using patchwork and ggtheme
text:
Creating composite figure using patchwork and ggtheme

patchwork <- ((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "1")
patchwork & theme_economist(dkpanel=TRUE) 














Tip



It is not possible to add both ggtheme and hrbrtheme as both as solid themes so adding both would result on the last theme added. For example if the code was pathwork & theme_economist() & theme_ipsum() the output will have the ipsum theme and no economist theme.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3 - Interactive Data Visualisation
text:
Tooltip effect
The code chunk below is a typical code chunk to plot an interactive statistical graph by using ggiraph package.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618
)











Note



Notice that the code chunk consists of two parts. First, an interactive version of ggplot object will be created. In this case, geom_dotplot_interactive() is used to create the basic graph. Next, girafe() of ggiraph will be used to create an interactive svg object to be displayed on an html page.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3 - Interactive Data Visualisation
text:
Displaying multiple information on tooltip
The content of the tooltip can be customized by including a list object as shown in the code chunk below.

exam_data$tooltip <- c(paste0(     
  "Name = ", exam_data$ID,         
  "\n Class = ", exam_data$CLASS)) 

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = exam_data$tooltip), 
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 8*0.618
)





The first 3 lines in the code is create a column called tooltip in Exam_data which is filled with the combined text of ID and CLASS values. Now this will act as the label for each student. Then this field is then called in line 7 tooltip = exam_data(tooltip) so that when building the chart it will use the new tooltip column instead.

Linked brushing
It is possible to create interactive coordinated visalisations where selecting data points in one widget automatically highlights or filters the corresponding data in another widget. Brush here mean click or drag to select data points in one chart. So a linked brushing means that by dragging to select data points in one chart, the same data points are simultaneously highlighted in another chart or table.

CodeOutput plot



d <- highlight_key(exam_data) 
p <- ggplot(d, 
            aes(ENGLISH,

  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))

                "plotly_selected")

                  DT::datatable(d), 
                  widths = 5)        







Note




highlight() is a function of plotly package. It sets a variety of optins for brushing multiple plots. These options are primarily designed for linking multuple ploly graphs, and may not behave as expected when linking plotly to another htmlwidget package via crosstalk. In some cases, other htmlwidgets will respect these options, such as persistent selection in leaflet.
bscols() is a helper function of crosstalk package It makes it easy to put HTML elements side by side. It can be called directly from the console but is especially designed to work in a R Markdown document. Warning: This will bring in all of Bootstrap!

text:
Plotting ridgeline graph using ggridges method
There are several ways to plot ridgeline plot with R. In this section, you will learn how to plot ridgeline plot by using ggridges package.
ggridges package provides two main geom to plot gridgeline plots, they are geom_ridgeline() and geom_density_ridges(). The former takes height values directlly to draw the ridgelines, and the latter first estimates data densitites and then draws those using ridgelines.
The code chunk below uses geom_density_ridges().

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#7097BB", .3),
    color = "white") +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, 
                   expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()

section: Varying fill colors along the x-axis
text:
Varying fill colors along the x-axis
Sometimes we would like to have the area under a ridgeline not filled with a single solid color but rather with colors that vary in some form along the x-axis. This effect can be achieved by using either geom_ridgeline_gradient() or geom_density_ridges_gradient(). Both geoms work just like geom_ridgeline() and geom_density_ridges(), except that they allow for varying fill colors. However, they do not allows for alpha transparency in the fill. For technical reasons, we can can eave changing fill colors or transpoarency but not both.

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Score",
                      option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous( name = "English grades", 
                      expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, 
                   expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()

The code chunk is plotted by mapping the probabilities calculated using stat(ecdf) which represent the empirical cumulative density function for the distribution of English score.

       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5-stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()

It is important to include argument calc_scdf = TRUE in stat_density_ridges().

                      quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()

  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
                      quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#FF0000A0", "#A0A0A0A0", "#0000FFA0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2 - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Correlation coefficient measures the type and strength of the relationship between two variables, ranging from -1 (perfect inverse relationship) to 1 (perfect positive relationship), with 0 indicating no linear relationship.
When working with multiple variables, these coefficients are arranged in a correlation matrix, which is used for three main purpose:

exploring pairwise relationships between variables
feeding into other analyses (like factor analysis or linear regression)
diagnosing issues in other analyses

For large datasets, a corrgram is a visual tool that displays correlations by representing their sign and magnitude, while also reordering variables so that similar ones appear together for easier pattern recognition.

Importing data
For this exercise, the Wine Quality Data Set of UCI Machine Leatning Reposutory will be used. The data set consists of 13 variables and 6497 observations.

wine <- read.csv("data/wine_quality.csv")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2 - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Basic correlation matrix
Figure below shows the scatter plot matrix of Wine quality Data in a 11 by 11 matrix.

pairs(wine[,1:11])








The required input of pairs() can be a matrix or data frame. The code chunk used to create the scatterplot matrix is relatively simple. It uses the default pairs function. The code chunk above uses column 1 to 11. The code chunk below uses column 12 to 12.

pairs(wine[,2:12])

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2 - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Drawing lower corner
pairs() function of R Graphics provided many customisation arguments. For exmaple, it is a common practice to show either the upper half or lower half of the correlation matrix instead of both. This is because a correlation matrix is symmetric.
To show the lower hald of the correlation matrix, the upper.panel argument will be used as shown in the code chunk below.

pairs(wine[,2:12], upper.panel = NULL)








Similarly, you can display the upper half of the correlation matrix instead by using the code chunk below.

pairs(wine[,2:12], lower.panel = NULL)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2 - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Including correlation coefficients
To show the correlation coefficient fo each pair of variables instead of scatter plot, panel.cor function will be used. This will also show higher correlations in a larger font.

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", cex.cor, ...) {
  usr <- par("usr")
  on.exit(par(usr))
  par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
  r <- abs(cor(x, y, use="complete.obs"))
  txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits=digits)[1]
  txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")
  if(missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8/strwidth(txt)
  text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1+r) / 2)
}

pairs(wine[,2:12], upper.panel = panel.cor)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2 - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Basic plot
One of the advantage of using ggcorrmat() over many other methods to visualise a correlation matrix is it’s ability o provide a comprehensive and yet professional statistical report as shown in the figure below.

ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  corr.vars = 1:11,
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black",
                         hc.order = TRUE,
                         tl.cex = 10),
  title = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
  subtitle = "Four pairs are no significant at p < 0.05"
)














Tip



Things to learn from the code chunk above: - cor.vars argument is used to compute the correlation matrix needed to build the corrgram - ggcorrplot.args argument provide additional (mostly aesthetic) arguments that will be passed to ggcorrplot::ggcorrplot function. The list should avoid any of the following arguments since they are already internally being used: corr, method, p.mat, sig.level, ggtheme, colors, lab, pch, legend.title, digits
The sample sub-code chunk can be used to control specific components of the plot such as the font size of the x-axis, y-axis, and the statistical report.

ggplot.component = list(
    theme(text=element_text(size=5),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8)))

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2 - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Getting started with corrplot
We need to comput the correlatin matrix of wine data frame first.

wine.cor <- cor(wine[, 1:11])

Next, corrplot() is used to plot the corrgram by using all the default setting as shown in the code chunk below.

corrplot(wine.cor)








Notice that the default visual object used to plot the corrgram is circle. The default layout of the corrgram is a symmetric matrix. The default colour scheme is diverging blue-red. Bkue colors are used to represent pair variables with positive correlation coefficients and red colors are used to represent pair variables with negative correlation coefficients. The intensity of the color or also known as saturation is used to represent the strength of the correlation coefficient. Darker colors indicate relatively stronger linear relationship between the paired variables. On the other hand, lighter colors indicate relatively weaker linear relationship.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2 - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Working with visual geometrics
In corrplot package, there are seven visual geometric (parameter method) can be used to encode the attribute values. They are: circle, square, ellipse, number, shade, color and pie. The default is circle. As shown in the previous section, the default visual geometric of corrplot matrix is circle. However, this default setting can be changed by using the method argument as shown in the code chunk below.

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2 - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Working with layout
corrplor() supports three layout types: “full”, “upper” or “lower”. The default is “full” which display full matrix. The default setting can be changed by using the type argument of corrplot().

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         type="lower")








The default layout of the corrgram can be further customised. For example, arguments diag and tl.col are used to turn off the diagonal cells and to change the axis text label color to black color respectively as shown in the code chunk and figure below.

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         type="lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black")














Tip



Other layout arguments that can be experimented on: tl.pos, tl.cex, tl.offset, cl.pos, cl.cex and cl.offset

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2 - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Working with mixed layout
With corrplot package, it is possible to design corrgram with mixed visual matrix of one half and numerical matrix on the other half. In order to create a coorgram with mized layout, the corrplot.mixed(), a wrapped function for mixed visualisation style will be used.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black")














Note



Notice that argument lower and upper are used to define the visualisation method used. In this case, ellipse is used to map the lower half of the corrgram and numerical matrix (i,e, number) is used to map the upper hald of the corrgram. The argument tl.pos, on the other hand, is used to specify the placement of the axis label. Lastly, the diag argument is used to specify the glyph on the principal diagonal of the corrgram.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2 - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Combinign corrgram with significant test.
In the statistical analysis, we are also interested to know which pair of variables their correlation coefficients are statistically significant.
With corrplot package, we can use the cor.mtest() to compute the p-values and confidence interval for eac pair of variables.

wine.sig = cor.mtest(wine.cor, conf.level= .95)

We can then use the p.mat argument of corrplot function as shown in the code chunk below.

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "number",
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45,
         p.mat = wine.sig$p,
         sig.level = .05)








As you can see, the corrgram reveals that not all correlation pairs are statically significant. For example the correlation between total sulfur dioxide and free sulfur dioxide is statistically significant at significant level of 0.1 but the not the pair between total sulfur dioxide and citric acid.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2 - Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Reorder a corrgram
Matrix reorder is very important for mining the hiden structure and pattern in corrgram. By default, the order of attributes of a corrgram is sorted according to the correlation matrix (i.e. “original”). The default setting can be over-write by using argument of corrplot(). Currently, corrplot package support four sorting methods, they are:

“AOE”: for angular order of the eigenvector
“FPC”:for the first principal component order
“hclust”: for hierarchical clustering order, and “hclust.method” for the agglomeration method to be used

“hclust.method” should be one of “ward”, “single”, “complete”, “average”, mcquitty”, “median” or “centroid”

“alphabet” for alphabetical order


AOEhclust



corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               order="AOE",
               tl.col = "black")










If using “hclust”, corrplot() can draw rectangle around the corrgram based on the results of hierarchical clustering.

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         tl.pos = "lt",
         tl.col = "black",
         order="hclust",
         hclust.method = "ward.D",
         addrect = 3)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 3 - Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
Data transformation
When analysing multivariate data set, it is very common that the variables in the data sets includes values that reflect different types of measurement. In general, these variables’ values have their own range. In order to ensure that all the variables have comparable values, data transformation are commonly used before clustering.
Three main data transformation methods are supported by heatmaply(): scale, normalise and percentilse.

Scaling methodNormalising methodPercentising method


When all variables are came from or assumed to come from some normal distribution, then scaling (i.e.: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation) would bring them all close to the standard normal distribution. In such a case, each value would reflect the distance from the mean in units of standard deviation.The scale argument in heatmaply() supports column and row scaling.
The code chunk below will scale variable values colume-wise.

heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)],
          scale = "column")







When variables in the data comes from possibly different (and non-normal) distributions, the normalize function can be used to bring data to the 0 to 1 scale by subtracting the minimum and dividing by the maximum of all observations. This preserves the shape of each variable’s distribution while making them easily comparable on the same “scale”.
Different from scaling, the normalise method is performed on the input data set i.e. wh_matrix as shown in the code chunk below.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))







This is similar to ranking the variables, but instead of keeping the rank values, divide them by the maximal rank. This is done by using the ecdf of the variables on their own values, bringing each value to its empirical percentile. The benefit of the percentize function is that each value has a relatively clear interpretation, it is the percent of observations that got that value or below it.
Similar to normalize method, the percentize method is also performed on the input data set i.e. wh_matrix as shown in the code chunk below.

heatmaply(percentize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))

text:
Clustering algorithm
heatmaply supports a variety of hierarchical clustering algorithm. The main arguments are:

distfun: function used to compute the distance (dissimilarity) between both rows and columns. Defaults to dist. The options “pearson”, “spearman” and “kendall” can be used to use correlation-based clustering, which uses as.dist(1 - cor(t(x))) as the distance metric (using the specified correlation method)
hclustfun: function used to compute the hierarchical clustering when Rowv or Colv are not dendrograms. Defaults to hclust
dist_method default is NULL, which results in “euclidean” to be used. It can accept alternative character strings indicating the method to be passed to distfun. By default distfun is “dist”” hence this can be one of “euclidean”, “maximum”, “manhattan”, “canberra”, “binary” or “minkowski”
hclust_method default is NULL, which results in “complete” method to be used. It can accept alternative character strings indicating the method to be passed to hclustfun. By default hclustfun is hclust hence this can be one of “ward.D”, “ward.D2”, “single”, “complete”, “average” (= UPGMA), “mcquitty” (= WPGMA), “median” (= WPGMC) or “centroid” (= UPGMC)

text:
Statistical approach
In order to determine the best clustering method and number of cluster the dend_expend() and find_k() functions of dendextend package will be used.
First, the dend_expend() will be used to determine the recommended clustering method to be used.

wh_d <- dist(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]), method = "euclidean")
dend_expend(wh_d)[[3]]

  dist_methods hclust_methods     optim
1      unknown         ward.D 0.6137851
2      unknown        ward.D2 0.6289186
3      unknown         single 0.4774362
4      unknown       complete 0.6434009
5      unknown        average 0.6701688
6      unknown       mcquitty 0.5020102
7      unknown         median 0.5901833
8      unknown       centroid 0.6338734


The output table shows that “average” method should be used because it gave the high optimum value.
Next, find_k() is used to determine the optimal number of cluster.

wh_clust <- hclust(wh_d, method = "average")
num_k <- find_k(wh_clust)
plot(num_k)








Figure above shows that k=3 would be good.
With reference to the statistical analysis results, we can prepare the code chunk as shown below.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "average",
          k_row = 3)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 3 - Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
Seriation
One of the problems with hierarchical clustering is that it doesn’t actually place the rows in a definite order, it merely constrains the space of possible orderings. Take three items A, B and C. If you ignore reflections, there are three possible orderings: ABC, ACB, BAC. If clustering them gives you ((A+B)+C) as a tree, you know that C can’t end up between A and B, but it doesn’t tell you which way to flip the A+B cluster. It doesn’t tell you if the ABC ordering will lead to a clearer-looking heatmap than the BAC ordering.
heatmaply uses the seriation package to find an optimal ordering of rows and columns. Optimal means to optimize the Hamiltonian path length that is restricted by the dendrogram structure. This, in other words, means to rotate the branches so that the sum of distances between each adjacent leaf (label) will be minimized. This is related to a restricted version of the travelling salesman problem.
Here we meet our first seriation algorithm: Optimal Leaf Ordering (OLO). This algorithm starts with the output of an agglomerative clustering algorithm and produces a unique ordering, one that flips the various branches of the dendrogram around so as to minimize the sum of dissimilarities between adjacent leaves. Here is the result of applying Optimal Leaf Ordering to the same clustering result as the heatmap above.

Default OLOGWMeanNone



heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "OLO")







“GW” (Gruvaeus and Wainer) which aims for the same goal but uses a potentially faster heuristic.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "GW")







The option “mean” gives the output we would get by default from heatmap functions in other packages such as gplots::heatmap.2.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "mean")







The option “none” gives us the dendrograms without any rotation that is based on the data matrix.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "none")

text:
pacman::p_load(treemap, treemapify, tidyverse) 




In this exercise, REALIS2018.csv data will be used. This dataset provides inormation of private propoerty transaction records in 2018.

realis2018 <- read_csv("data/realis2018.csv")




The data.frame realis2018 is in trasaction record form, which is highly disaggregated and not appropriate to be used to plot a treemap. In this section, we will perform the following steps to manipulate and prepare a data.frtame that is appropriate for treemap visualisation:

group transaction records by Project Name, Planning Region, Planning Area, Property Type and Type of Sale
compute Total Unit Sold, Total Area, Median Unit Price and Median Transacted Price by applying appropriate summary statistics on No. of Units, Area (sqm), Unit Price ($ psm) and Transacted Price ($) respectively.

Two key verbs of dplyr package, namely: group_by() and summarize() will be used to perform these steps.
group_by() breaks down a data.frame into specified groups of rows. When you then apply the verbs above on the resulting object they’ll be automatically applied “by group”.
Grouping affects the verbs as follows:

grouped select() is the same as ungrouped select(), except that grouping variables are always retaine
grouped arrange() is the same as ungrouped; unless you set .by_group = TRUE, in which case it orders first by the grouping variables
mutate() and filter() are most useful in conjunction with window functions (like rank(), or min(x) == x)
sample_n() and sample_frac() sample the specified number/fraction of rows in each group
summarise() computes the summary for each group

In our case, group_by() will used together with summarise() to derive the summarised data.frame.



The code chunk below shows a typical two lines code approach to perform the steps.

realis2018_grouped <- group_by(
  realis2018, `Project Name`,`Planning Region`, 
  `Planning Area`, `Property Type`, `Type of Sale`)
realis2018_summarised <- summarise(
  realis2018_grouped, `Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
  `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
  `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE), 
  `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))







Note



Aggregation functions such as sum() and meadian() obey the usual rule of missing values: if there’s any missing value in the input, the output will be a missing value. The argument na.rm = TRUE removes the missing values prior to computation.





The code chunk below shows a more efficient way to tackle the same processes by using the pipe.

realis2018_summarised <- realis2018 %>% 
  group_by(`Project Name`,`Planning Region`, 
           `Planning Area`, `Property Type`, 
           `Type of Sale`) %>%
  summarise(`Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))

Design static treemap
In this section, treemap() of Treemap package is used to plot a treemap showing the distribution of median unit prices and total unit sold of resale condominium by geographic hierarchy in 2017.
First, we will select records belongs to resale condominium property type from realis2018_selected data frame.

text:
Using basic arguments
The code chunk below designed a treemap by using three core arguments of treemap(): index, vSize and vColor.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )














Tip



Things to learn:

index

The index vector must consist of at least two column names or else no hierarchy treemap will be plotted
If multiple column names are provided, such as the code chunk above, the first name is the highest aggregation level, the second highest aggregation level, and so on

vSize

The column must not contain negative values. This is because it’s values will be used to map the sizes of the rectangles of the treemaps










Warning



The treemap above was wrongly colored. For a correctly designed treemap, the colors of the rectangles should be in different intensity showing, in our case, median unit prices.
For treemap(), vColor is used in combination with the argument type to determines the colors of the rectangles. Without defining type, like the code chunk above, treemap() assumes type = index, in our case, the hierarchy of planning areas.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 5 - Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
Colors in treemap package
There are two arguments that determine the mapping to color palettes: mapping and palette. The only difference between “value” and “manual” is the default value for mapping. The “value” treemap considers palette to be a diverging color palette (say ColorBrewer’s “RdYlBu”), and maps it in such a way that 0 corresponds to the middle color (typically white or yellow), -max(abs(values)) to the left-end color, and max(abs(values)), to the right-end color. The “manual” treemap simply maps min(values) to the left-end color, max(values) to the right-end color, and mean(range(values)) to the middle color.

        )

Although the color palette used is RdYlBu but there are no red rectangles in the treemap above. This is because all the median unit prices are positive
The reason why we see only 5000 to 45000 in the legend is because the range argument is by default c(min(values, max(values)) with some pretty rounding

The “manual” type treemap
The “manual” type does not interpret the values as the “value” type does. Instead, the value range is mapped linearly to the color palette.

To overcome this problem, a single color palette such as Blues should be used

Treemap layout
treemap() supports two popular treemap layouts, namely: “squarified” and “pivotSize”. The default is “pivotSize”.
The squarified treemap algorithm produces good aspect ratios, but ignores the sorting order of the rectangles (sortID). The ordered treemap, pivot-by-size, algorithm takes the sorting order (sortID) into account while aspect ratios are still acceptable.

text:
Combining corrgram with significant test.
In the statistical analysis, we are also interested to know which pair of variables their correlation coefficients are statistically significant.
With corrplot package, we can use the cor.mtest() to compute the p-values and confidence interval for eac pair of variables.

wine.sig = cor.mtest(wine.cor, conf.level= .95)

We can then use the p.mat argument of corrplot function as shown in the code chunk below.

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "number",
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45,
         p.mat = wine.sig$p,
         sig.level = .05)








As you can see, the corrgram reveals that not all correlation pairs are statically significant. For example the correlation between total sulfur dioxide and free sulfur dioxide is statistically significant at significant level of 0.1 but the not the pair between total sulfur dioxide and citric acid.

driving_experience
driving_experience is needed to get how long the driver has been driving for, which is more meaningful as compared to the age when the driver receives the driving licence.
First check if age_driving_licence means the year driving licence is issued or the age the driver got the driving licence.

  select(driver_age, age_driving_licence, year)

# A tibble: 1 × 3

       <dbl>               <dbl> <dbl>
1         82                  80  2024


Combining with the first row value shown in the head summary, it can be concluded that age_driving_licence is the age of the driver when driving licence is issued. Hence to get driving_experience the formula should be driver_age - age_driving_licence.

insurance <- insurance %>%
  mutate(driving_experience = 
           driver_age - age_driving_licence)



loss_ratio
This feature will show the ratio of total_incurred to total_premium. This is important as it is the standard insurance profitability metric.

insurance <- insurance %>%
  mutate(loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium)

Relationship between years of driving experience and profitability
Since driving experience is a numeric value, the test done should be a Significant Test of Correlation. This is done using ggscatterplot. Looking at the univariate analysis, even though driving_experience is normally distributed, loss_ratio is very skewed. So the non-parametric version is used instead, which is the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient.

ggscatterstats(

  x = driving_experience,
  y = loss_ratio,
  type = "nonparametric",
  title = "Relationship between years of driving experience and profitability"
)
